source.text:
Many responses will be straw dogs about trades are universally all physically disabling. If you're a crane operator and you're trying to lift 175 tons with your own knees and back, you're doing it wrong. Its easy to find trades jobs in almost any environment. There are physically punishing jobs like roofer or concrete work, but that does not somehow prove all the other jobs are debilitating.

Many people die young and fat and very sick at desk jobs. Inertness does not seem to equal health. A job like industrial maint electrician involves just enough walking around to outlive the average desk jockey. Of course there are very fat and sick heavy equipment operators...

Another meme response you'll get implies its all your choice to "stay in" whereas the problem is the market is contracting so fast you won't be allowed in if you're not already in, and if you're kicked out (layoff, just not keeping on the official mandatory career path, etc) you'll never ever get back in. Don't worry about deciding to leave software development, plan ahead for when you're uncontrollably permanently kicked out. Its not going to be your decision.

Education can be helpful on the jobsite. I've seen fine finish woodworkers do very weird, yet successful, graphical solutions to avoid five seconds of trigonometry. Automation PLC programmers will do weird stuff to avoid bode plots and similar control theory topics. There are people tuning PID controllers on the job who don't know or understand the P, I or D, they just twiddle the knobs until it works right, often while developing all sorts of magical mythology.

Keep in mind the wide spectrum of the size of your counterparty. Working for a multinational megacorporation at a mine operating heavy equipment for your entire career will be wildly different experience from working for a single human individual digging a septic field for a day.

An interesting analogy with lawyers is people like to think their interface is like a chatbot so a chatbot will replace them. But people actually HIRE lawyers because they want to outsource the risks of doing something legal-related to someone else, in a way its an insurance gig not a chatbot gig. You'll find in the trades they're not really hiring a guy to move the levers to dig a trench, they're outsourcing the risk and hassle of owning your own excavator machine and the risks of screwed up one-call utility marking, etc. In a similar way a robot arm that can screw a wire to a wall switch won't replace an electrician who knows how to run wires without taking an axe to every piece of plaster in the room. Its fascinating how the invention of CNC machines has not resulted in machine shops closing down and every company broom closet having their own personal robot mill and lathe, but it has changed the entire experience of working at a machine shop... See also 3d printing LOL.
